newsitem.title: USA: TWA crash probers lean toward mechanical fault.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash probers lean toward mechanical fault.

text.p: One of the lead investigators into the crash of TWA Flight 800 said on Thursday that with only 5 percent of the doomed jetliner yet to be recovered, there was a "mathematical logic" to ruling out sabotage.

National Transportation Safety Board vice-chairman Robert Francis also said in a CNN television interview it was "real disappointing and not normal" to be so far into an air disaster investigation without knowing what caused it.

The Boeing 747 exploded in mid-air and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off New York's Long Island on July 17, just minutes after taking off from John F. Kennedy airport on a flight to Paris. All 230 people on board were kiled.
In the four months since the crash, investigators have given equal weight to three theories -- that a bomb, a missile or catastrophic mechanical failure brought down the plane.

Asked whether he now thought it was less likely that evidence of a bomb or missile would emerge, Francis said, "I think there's some mathematical logic to that but I would say also that I don't think (we) would rule out the possibility that one could still find those options."

His remarks were similar to those FBI assistant director James Kallstrom made to New York newspapers. "It is like searching your 10-room house for your keys, and you have searched nine rooms and haven't found them and you say it is less likely than when you started that you'll find your keys," said Kallstrom, who has spearheaded the criminal investigation into the crash.

Francis said four scalloping boats were dredging out the remaining bits and pieces of the aircraft some 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) under the silt on the ocean floor. He said most of what was being recovered was easily identified. The bodies or remains of 215 of the 230 victims have been recovered.

Investigators know the centre fuel tank of the jumbo jet exploded but have not determined what caused the blast. Francis said his agency was "working with Boeing and FAA (the Federal Aviation Administration) with the centre fuel tank situation but we won't mandate anything until we know what happened."
